analysisMarkdown:
## Where the price sits

Spot gold trades at **$3,556.09**, down **2.27%** on the day. That leaves it **35.3% below** its 52-week high of **$5,496** (set on 2026-01-29) and barely above its 52-week low of **$3,533**, recorded on 2026-11-21. This is not record territory — it is the lower end of a steep, multi-month decline. Gold is **10.9% below** its 50-day average ($3,990) and **15.8% below** its 200-day average ($4,223). Trailing returns are negative across the board: **-9.8%** over 20 days, **-23.5%** over 90 days, and **-14.1%** over the past year. Annualised 20-day volatility of **33%** confirms an unsettled, fast-moving tape, with the 20-day closing range spanning $3,533 to $4,121.

## The macro backdrop

The pressure on gold is coming squarely from the macro side. The Federal Reserve's trade-weighted **broad dollar index** sits at **123.60**, higher than **100%** of readings in the past year and up **2.26** points over 30 days. A dollar at a one-year high makes dollar-priced gold more expensive for the rest of the world and typically weighs on the metal. The **10-year real yield** is **2.77%**, higher than **91%** of past-year readings and up **0.37 pp** over 90 days — a meaningful headwind, since a higher real return on inflation-protected bonds raises the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding gold. The nominal **10-year Treasury yield** is **4.92%**, while the **10-year inflation breakeven** has eased to **2.15%**, down 0.22 pp over 30 days. Falling breakevens blunt gold's inflation-hedge appeal.

## Short-term scorecard (1–4 weeks)

The short-term scorecard reads **-4**, a baseline **SELL**. In plain language: the 20-day return of -9.8% is strongly adverse, and the price trading 10.9% below its 50-day average is adverse. The one offsetting factor is contrarian — that same stretch below the 50-day average can count *for* a rebound — but it is outweighed. The 30-day change in the real yield is roughly flat (neutral), while the broad dollar's 1.86% rise over 30 days is strongly adverse. The standing SELL call has been in place since 2026-11-16.

## Long-term scorecard (3–12 months)

The long-term scorecard is uniformly negative at **-6**, also a baseline **SELL**, carried at high confidence. Every component points the same way: spot is 15.8% below the 200-day average; the 50-day average sits 5.5% below the 200-day (a bearish trend structure); the 90-day return is -23.5%; the price is 35.3% below its 52-week high; the real yield has risen 0.37 pp over 90 days; and the broad dollar has gained 4.69% over 90 days. There is no measured tailwind on this horizon.

## Events driving the market

- **Fed rate-hike expectations.** The decisive catalyst has been a shift toward a near-certain December Fed hike. Reports on 2026-11-18 described gold breaking below $3,800 to a 14-month low as firmer rate-hike odds lifted the dollar.
- **Dollar and yields.** As of 2026-11-20, a broad dollar at a one-year high and elevated real yields coincided with gold slipping toward $3,500.
- **AI-driven equity selloff.** On 2026-11-23, an unwinding of leveraged technology positions forced investors to sell gold and silver to raise cash, complicating the metal's traditional safe-haven role — even as a brief relief rally lifted prices above $3,600 before today's reversal.
- **Softer inflation expectations.** Cooling breakevens reduce gold's inflation-hedge demand over the longer horizon.

## Short-term outlook

Over the next **1–4 weeks**, conditions look more challenging than supportive. Negative momentum, a price well below the 50-day average, and a dollar at a one-year high dominate. The November 23 bounce above $3,600 showed that oversold rallies can be sharp, but it has already faded. The standing SELL would be challenged by a **daily close above $4,121**.

## Long-term outlook

Over **3–12 months**, the trend, valuation-versus-averages and macro signals all align to the downside. Gold would need to repair a great deal of technical damage to shift this reading; the call would be challenged by a **daily close above $4,673**.

## Risks to the view

The main risk to the bearish setup is a policy pivot: if the AI-driven equity stress deepens and reshapes the Fed outlook toward easing rather than hiking, the dollar and real yields could reverse, removing gold's biggest headwinds quickly. Standing official-sector demand remains a backdrop, but it is not a dated catalyst here. Conversely, if December hike expectations harden further, the dollar and real yields could extend, keeping pressure on the price. Given 33% annualised volatility, moves in either direction may be outsized.
